THOUGHT: The patient is a 31-year-old woman with a 5-month history of intermittent flank pain and recurrent UTIs (5 episodes in 2 years). Key physical findings include bilateral nontender upper abdominal masses, bilateral flank dullness, and palpable renal masses — highly suggestive of enlarged kidneys. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated BUN (29 mg/dL) and creatinine (1.4 mg/dL), indicating impaired kidney function. Renal ultrasound reveals “bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multiple parenchymal anechoic masses” — classic imaging appearance of cysts. Anechoic, well-defined, round renal masses in a young adult with preserved or near-normal baseline health point strongly to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Although ADPKD typically presents in the 3rd–4th decade with hypertension, flank pain, hematuria, or renal insufficiency — and often has a positive family history — *de novo* mutations occur, and ~10–15% of cases lack a known family history. Her hypertension (BP 150/88 mmHg) is consistent with early ADPKD-related renin-mediated hypertension. Recurrent UTIs may reflect urinary stasis or cyst infection — a known complication of ADPKD. Other considerations (e.g., medullary sponge kidney, acquired cystic kidney disease, or malignancy) are less likely: medullary sponge kidney usually presents with nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis and normal-sized kidneys; acquired cystic disease occurs in end-stage renal disease (not applicable here); and solid or complex masses would raise concern for malignancy — but the report specifies *anechoic* (i.e., simple, fluid-filled) cysts. No evidence of systemic illness, fever, or inflammatory markers to suggest infection or vasculitis.

DIAGNOSIS: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
